title: Love all creation
hook: Dostoevsky's Zosima: love every leaf, every ray of light, the animals, the plants
tomorrow: what if you're too small for the stairs everyone else climbs?

segments.voice: Yesterday Hopkins saw a worn world still charged with grandeur. Today closes the week, and it closes small: one leaf at a time.

A weed pushing out of a sidewalk crack. A spider in the corner of the shower. A dog that isn't yours, waiting outside a store. How small can a thing be and still be worth loving? In a long Russian novel, an old monk answers by naming things that small. Love all God's creation, he says, every grain of sand. Love every leaf, every ray of God's light. Love the animals, love the plants, love everything.
screen: `A WEED, A SPIDER, A STRANGER'S DOG.` → `HOW SMALL IS TOO SMALL?` → `EVERY GRAIN OF SAND.`

segments.voice: The monk is Father Zosima, in Dostoevsky's The Brothers Karamazov. He's a novelist's character, so the novel itself is the source. His reason is the surprise: love everything, and you'll begin to perceive God's mystery in things. Love first; the seeing follows. Underneath is the first page of the Bible, in Genesis: “God saw every thing that he had made, and, behold, it was very good.” Zosima's love agrees with that verdict, one leaf at a time. Not nature as an idea. A single leaf, with a torn edge and a stem. Now hold the whole week up to the light. A spiritual's question at the cross, answered with trembling. A deep river, and home gathered on the far side. A pilgrim asking how to pray always, and a prayer that learned to pray itself. A poet with empty hands who gave her heart. A worn world, charged with grandeur. And today, every leaf. Songs, a pilgrim, two poets and a novelist, each pointing past its own page.
screen: `ZOSIMA, A MONK IN A NOVEL.` · `LOVE FIRST; THE SEEING FOLLOWS.` · `VERY GOOD, ONE LEAF AT A TIME.` · `A WEEK OF VOICES.` · then, large: `LOVE EVERY LEAF.`

segments.voice: If there's a plant, a leaf or a flower within reach, hold it, or bring your face close and breathe in its smell. Find one detail you'd never notice in passing: a vein, a torn edge, a speck of dust. Stay with that one living thing for the whole sit, as if it were the only one.
Love all creation. Zosima's teaching in Dostoevsky's novel: love every part of what God made, down to the leaf.
The line for this week's end: love every leaf. Not nature in general; one leaf, with a torn edge. Seven days, done.

fork.setup: your little sister wants to stomp an ant hill "because they're just bugs." which sentence fits Zosima's teaching?
options: "they're tiny, but they're part of what God made. let's watch them instead."
"leave them alone, or they'll bite you and it'll hurt."
"only people matter to God, but stomping is still kind of mean."
fork.reveal: Zosima says love every leaf, the animals, everything, as God's creation. Genesis calls all of it very good.

chat.says: Pop's PT is walking to the mailbox. takes forever, he stops at every flower. i'm so impatient
options: Slow down with him. Zosima says love every leaf; he's seeing what we rush past.
Gently hurry him. Loving creation is nice, but his recovery comes first.
Bring headphones. Let him look while you get your own stuff done.
chat.meaning: Zosima says love every leaf, and the seeing follows the love. Walking at Pop's pace lets you see what he's seeing.
